<reason>Side A (PRO) built and defended a coherent comparative case: speed-as-severity physics conceded by CON, certainty-of-enforcement over severity, durable national rollouts (France, Britain, NYC), and the unique externality of armed roadside encounters. Side A's rebuttals repeatedly flipped CON's own arguments (patrol cars as "temporary spots," variance compression, repeal-as-proof-of-efficacy) and answered pressure directly (Finland/Switzerland income-scaled fines; checkpoints as bonus, not dependency). Side B landed real hits—the checkpoint contradiction in B2.3, the clever 2020-spike reframing in B4.1, and the "zero hit rate" closing frame—but its decisive claims were overstated: "speed is the variable that kills least often" contradicts both physics and B's own opening concession, and the severity argument blunts the blindness attack since cameras reduce harm even from drivers they cannot identify. B's "single digits, at best" admission was costly and A leveraged it into the hit-rate arithmetic. The surveillance externality went unanswered until A's closing, but A's plate-readers-already-exist answer was adequate. Both sides had one clipped turn (execution cost each). A wins on both prongs of the motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 1 reversal that a patrol car is merely a "temporary spot" while a fixed camera is permanent, plus the average-speed-corridor fix, neutralized B's core "spot effects" attack in B1.2. Side B's best moment was catching that A's sobriety-checkpoint credit [A2.7] relied on the very stop-based enforcement the motion compares against [B2.3], though A's "bonus, not dependency" clarification contained the damage.</best_rebuttal>
